This is truly as good as everybody says, it is not overhyped. First, every set of levels has a unique puzzle element, and the levels are designed to very cleverly make use of this puzzle element to solve the level. The game is both hard and fun. Because you can come back later for some things, even though the puzzles are hard, you don't have to get stuck there. 

Another thing is that the whole game revolves around a fairly layered and interesting story. There's the main story, the releationship allegory, and a deeper set of references... This is a great game.

Sometimes, when watching a film or reading a novel, you feel a burn of emotion deep inside your chest. Something that affects you so profoundly that it moves beyond being just a form of media. It is internalized and remembered forever.

Braid is one of those things. But it isn't just an example of art in gaming, it's a game full of pure genius as well.

The game, at first, comes off as a platformer. There are relatively little instances of hardcore platforming in the game, and they usually only serve as a medium to allow you to interact with the puzzle that you're dealing with. Make no mistake, this is a puzzle game at heart.

The puzzles here are incredibly good, and very well scaled from level to level. The first two levels are relatively easy and will only take you a few minutes, the third is a bit harder, and the last puzzles will make you feel like your brain is deflated. The amount of time that you'll have to put into each puzzle may be debilitating for some, but the sheer joy and pleasure of solving one overcomes any sense of stress that staring at your screen racking your brain may cause. These aren't just run of the mill puzzles, either. There are a number that are, in my mind, some of the best puzzles that I've ever seen in a game.

The art direction is beautiful. The backgrounds are watercolor constructed, they're vibrant and bright, and dark and brooding. The soundtrack is perfectly placed and flooded with beautiful violin work. Each are augmented by an incredibly written preface that comes prior to starting each level. The story is written so broadly and so metaphorically that it can literally be translated to represent whatever the player would like it to. The ending represents one of the epic twists in video game history, and does so in game -- a puzzle in itself.

I literally cannot think of one thing that I dislike about this game. It could be longer, but length can't really be expected from a game that costs so little.

There is so much value stuffed into the 10ish hours that you'll spend playing this game, it's hard to put it into words any other way than just to spout off the cliche of "buy it and experience it yourself". It's an experience to be had, and it's one of the most artistically beautiful exhibits in gaming history that is guaranteed to affect you in a most profound way.
Did you really delist the original, still fully functional version of Braid from Steam just to divert people towards buying the superfluous, more expensive remake? Bold strategy.

[h1]REVIEW[/h1]
[b]Braid[/b] is a short and sweet puzzle/platformer with an quasi-innovative time-manipulation aspect.  The ability to rewind time not only allows for intriguing gameplay, but also provides a good way for there to be challenging puzzles without the game becoming unnecessarily frustrating. If you like puzzle/platformers, this should be high on your list of games to try.

The game mixes elements of puzzlers and platforming to form its identity. And there is a comfortable familiarity to the game which should feel inviting to most gamers. It starts off mostly focused on thinking-based puzzles and then a little while into the game there does start to be some platforming aspects sprinkled in, where your reaction time and precision abilities will be tested.  But for the most part it's pretty mild and not that hard.  Again, the time-manipulation also helps alleviate some of the difficulty of the platforming sections. It works out so a large majority of people should have an easy time enjoying [b]Braid.[/b]

And as you progress through the game you will unlock different time-manipulation abilities which will need to be used properly to complete your quest. So the gameplay evolves throughout the campaign, keeping things fresh and keeping your mind active.

There isn't much of a story to be mentioned, but the game doesn't really need one. There is a strong influence of old school platformers (i.e.: the early [i]Mario Bros.[/i] games). In that vein, there is a basic purpose to your actions, but no need for a sprawling narrative.  Your quest in [b]Braid[/b] is to traverse hostile lands to rescue a kidnapped princess, what else do you really need to know. Also, there isn’t that much of an immersive atmosphere either. The ambiance feels very nondescript and purely functional. However, none of this is a bad thing; [b]Braid[/b] is simply a game that is focused on gameplay, purposefully minimizing the other distractive aspects.

And so I definitely recommend you check out [b]Braid[/b] if you’re a fan of the puzzle/platformer genre and are looking for a new game that focuses on gameplay. Also if you are someone who loves a real challenge, the speed-run achievement can give you a nice "run for your money.”

Braid is a platforming puzzle game which was released on Xbox Live initially in 2008 before later being ported onto PC in 2009.  You play the character, Tim, as you attempt to rescue the princess from a monster (very cliche!). 

Game play in Braid looks like a very generic puzzle platformer on face value, however with the addition of the special ability to manipulate time by rewinding and fast forwarding, you can find yourself in some very unique situations.  The other gameplay elements are very much the same though, running, jumping and climbing around a standard platforming environment.  Each level in the game adds a little bit of a change to the time bending ability which keeps things fresh each time you progress.  

Braid is a very simple looking game; the graphics are standard two 2D style, however they do have a very pleasing charm to it. The art style within the game is just gorgeous to look at. The art work alone apparently took over a year to produce, and you can really tell a huge amount of heart and effort went into creating it. 

The plot in Braid is very intriguing indeed. You are certainly in for a few twists and turns and very unpredictable outcomes throughout - I was personally in no way shape or form expecting the end of the game to end up how it did; and that is a nice change from a game since they can sometimes become very predictable. After finishing the game, you are able to find additional text that expand the story even further too. 

The music used in Braid was selected by the developer himself, from licensed music, this was done to reduce the cost in the development stage. What I really liked about the music is that each tune has a different feel to it when you re-wind time in game; its a really small element, but it makes a huge difference to how you feel when playing. 

I found Braid to be a difficult game; purely because I am the worst person possible when it comes to 1) Puzzles and 2) Platformers. Put the two together and it's just a mess.  At times I had to resort to a trusty walkthrough to work it out, but for the majority of the time I was able to figure out each level on my own. Puzzle veterans may well find this game's puzzles to be easy, and still struggle on the platforming element to it!

Braid took me just over six hour to complete; this was purely a run through the story mode; there are a lot of Jigsaw pieces to find in the game which result in achievements, so will add a couple more hours of gameplay. Some of which are unobtainable at the first time of coming across them, so a little bit of replaying older levels is needed to collect them all. However I personally see no reason to replay the game only for the achievements.  The story and gameplay 100% linear. 

I had no technical problems whilst playing. Braid can be played at all resolutions up to 4k in windowed mode and full screen. A controller, as always with platformers is highly recommended to play but can also be played with keyboard. 

To sum up, I am only going to Recommend Braid, simply because the two genres put together are my least favorite of all time, however take that with a pinch of salt because if you really enjoy puzzle/platformers, then this game is certainly for you and you need to pick it up, even at the full price of £6,99 this game is a steal!

An intellectually stimulating combination of symbolic game design, brilliant visuals, an immersive soundtrack, and a post-modern story that will leave you pondering its implications for months. I consider this the best videogame ever made.

I've become increasingly interested in video games as a form of art, and that was how this game appeared to me before playing. Now that I have played it, I'm certain it's a necessary part of that artistic conversation. Like any great piece of fiction, it has solid themes that are ambiguous in interpretation, those being time and regret. Unlike art in other mediums, it is able to make the player live those themes, and each puzzle is not only interesting and satisfying, but also thematically relevant. In one puzzle, as a basic example, you must sacrifice a past version of yourself to move forward. It isn't just imagery or metaphor as it would be in another medium, it is something the player must figure they must do before executing it themselves. That is the power of games as art.

Braid also works as a subversion of video game tropes, but I think the way it does so (especially in that brilliant final level) are so surprising that you should figure that out on your own. I've heard this game called pretentious and I genuinely can't understand that viewpoint: if you aren't remotely interested in art AND you don't feel like challenging yourself to mind-bending puzzles, I guess you shouldn't pick this one up. But if you look for meaning, you will find it here.

[h1] Overthinking Emotions [/h1]

This story is so weird, man. It feels like a very intelligent developer had a sad loss of his loved girl in his real life, couldn't cope with it so made many many weird thoughts on it about time going backwards and put everything of that into this game. Sentences like "He cut rats into pieces to examine their brains, implanted tungsten posts into the skulls of water-starved monkeys." made me go "wtf is wrong with this dev"? In my life I noticed that the more intelligent people are, the more thoughts they are producing, because they are capable of it, capable of processing more information, more possibilities, more "what-if"s. Often they get lost in their brain in a labyrinth of thoughts of alternate realities. Then, living in the simple not so interesting, not so thought-challenging reality of other more simple humans becomes very hard or even unbearable, because noone can follow you being off into the thought cloud. But it's cozy there using all your brain CPU power and stressful in real life running in subchallenging "what's the point of wasting my time with this" low clock speed. It seems to me, that the world of this man gifted with a very performant brain CPU clashed with the oh so confusing and irrational world of emotional social life and this clash produced this game.

Anyway, the game itself holds very interesting and unique time mechanics I ever saw in a puzzle game. It's not very long, but what is there makes you go scratch your head a lot. Reversing time, time alter excluding areas, alternate realities, time speed depending on item location and even more. Getting all puzzle pieces will take you a good while. It took me 4 hours. The game can be completed in under 45 minutes. I consider it a very unique gem of indie games history.

I watched Indie Game: The Movie and bought this game on sale. After about 4 hours, I did everything except for the speedruns, which I decided weren’t worth my time.

The story just seems all over the place, I know it's supposed to be out of order, but what order is it supposed to be in exactly? Reading through the texts, almost nothing seemed to be part of some cohesive story line and nothing was even enjoyable to read. What a terrible epilogue. Far before the end of the game, I had lost all interest in the story, which comes off as pretentious.

Puzzle difficulty increases almost exponentially, which would be fine if there was more instruction on your new powers than just "The Pit" levels at the beginning of each world, especially with the ring.

The art is also very off-putting to me. The main character, Tim, has this unsettling stare up into the sky, like he’s looking at nothing and his expressions consist of a creepy toothless smile and what looks like a frown maybe? One of the puzzles has the gall to make use of the jigsaw puzzle pieces scattered throughout the game, as if the bland looking platforms are distinct somehow.

Most of the music was good, at least the first time I heard it. In world 4, since your movements change time, each level is really only about 8-20 seconds of real music and you get to hear it all distorted and weird for like 30 minutes as you struggle through the puzzles.

This game was enjoyable for about 45 minutes and I don’t recommend buying it at full price under any circumstance.

Edit: I have since read the Wikipedia article about this game and it just about validates every single problem I had with this game. Blow basically says outright that the story is whatever you thought it was (in my case it was trash). Blow was so pretentious about his game that he didn't think anyone was smart enough to make a soundtrack for it. And again, Tim looks like Chucky.

I have also realized that this game is, in fact, not at all as intelligent as it is made out to be. Just because you can't understand something, doesn't make it smart, it doesn't make it a masterpiece. If you want to ponder and reflect on a story, read a goddamn book, don't play this game.

This is a masterpiece of game design. The puzzles constantly troll you when you go into a natural rhythm, forcing you to rethink your approach and choose a path that might not always seem obvious. The visuals and sound are all very atmospheric and still hold up after 8+ years. My main criticism is that the ending is only unlocked after you've finished all of the puzzle pieces from the whole world, which can be a little irritating if you're stuck on a puzzle for a little while. Still, every puzzle (except for 1 in the first world) presents you with what you need to complete it, so you're never left wondering if there's something that you're missing a critical component. Overall, an amazing game and truly ahead of its (and our) time.

Braid is a puzzle game masquerading as a platformer. Once you know the solutions to the puzzles, solving them requires no more effort than, say, setting up a combo in Puyo Puyo. But figuring out the solutions can be tough.

The game starts off easy, but forces you to stretch your thinking in order to proceed. I like how each section requires you to think in a totally different way. Some sections require you think of time as a changeable element you can rewind, others define space, and your place in it, as the wild card. Solving these puzzles evokes the good feeling you get when finishing a big jigsaw puzzle, and it's a joy to look at.

It has a major design drawback: the small written descriptions of the plot that flash onto the screen as you pass books on the way to the level doors. I know a lot of people have responded to positively to the story of this game, but in my opinion the overwrought prose really harms the otherwise subtle and sad imagery you encounter in the levels. The images should be all you need. It's a small point, I guess, since you can ignore the words, but they mar an otherwise excellent experience for me.

This game is not really well-optimized. On my last computer, the game struggled to maintain 15 fps in windowed mode. If you have a newer computer you should be fine, but keep it in mind.

[h1] Revisiting 'Braid': A Timeless Odyssey in Gaming [/h1]

Over a decade has passed since "Braid" graced our screens, setting the gaming world ablaze with its surreal, cerebral, and retrograde charm. In an era dominated by blockbuster releases, this indie gem stood out as a critical darling, instantly catapulting its creator, Jonathan Blow, into millionaire status.

What made "Braid" such a standout? Well, it arrived at the perfect moment. As an Xbox Live Arcade exclusive, it marked a shift towards downloadable content and the rise of independently developed games. It was an era where video games were becoming more than just discs you bought at a store - they were evolving into digital experiences you downloaded onto your console.

"Braid" was not just a game; it was a statement about what video games could be. It introduced players to Tim, a seemingly ordinary protagonist, clad in a business suit. Tim had a unique ability: he could manipulate time, reversing it whenever he wished. Death was no longer a threat; instead, the challenge lay in using this power to solve intricate puzzles across 38 levels.

The story in "Braid" starts simply: Tim is on a quest to rescue a princess. However, it's the climax that elevates this game from a puzzler to a thought-provoking narrative. When Tim finally reaches the princess, the game rewinds, revealing that she had been fleeing from him all along, setting traps to deter his advances.

The interpretation of this twist varies. Some see it as commentary on toxic masculinity, while others delve into deeper meanings, like the creation of the atomic bomb. Blow, the enigmatic developer, refuses to clarify the game's message, leaving players to decipher it themselves.

Blow's reluctance to provide definitive answers is admirable. He expects players to solve the game's puzzles, and the story's meaning is the most significant puzzle of all. This obscurity is one of the game's most intriguing aspects.

In my view, the straightforward explanation - a commentary on the way video games often diminish female characters and how male gamers perceive themselves as heroes in selfish narratives - holds significant weight. It's a reflection on the gaming culture that feels even more pertinent today.

"Braid" excels because its themes are interwoven with its gameplay, deconstructing video games and gamers themselves. Yet, Blow's insistence on telling gamers they've misunderstood the game might be its chief flaw. In the realm of video games, individual experiences reign supreme. Players interpret games differently, and that's part of the beauty.

Ultimately, "Braid" challenges us to accept that players won't always see games as developers intended. And that's a puzzle worth embracing.

Delisted from Steam. If only we could rewind back in time and buy the original game again...
A rather hypocritical and seemingly desperate move from its creator.

When the great movie critic Roger Ebert said that videogames are not, and will never be art, half the Internet rushed to convince him otherwise. Braid was one of the games they showed him as examples of art in form of videogames. He dismissed it saying he's not "persuaded that I can learn about my own past by taking back my mistakes in a video game", and called the story "prose on the level of a wordy fortune cookie".
There was hardly a worse choice of game to show the movie critic -- not because it's a bad game, but because it relies heavily on hundreds of hours of other games' experience, playing with it, twisting the familiar mechanics, betraying the expectations and subverting the rules. Hours that Ebert obviously never experienced, so the words like "Your princess is in another castle" meant nothing for them, and the subversion that came with them (I'm not going to spoil that) never connected to anything.
I'm not sure what the game's true story is -- it might be about the atomic bomb, or about a creepy stalker with a crush, or about time travel. What I'm sure is, it's about these hours we've spent playing Mario that suddenly turn inside out, showing that what once used to be a simple kid's fun can work as a mature artistsic medium, telling stories and bringing up emotion without a single line of text.

If you're like me, here's what you do:

1. Buy and install Braid
2. Traverse through the worlds without solving them
3. Wonder why the game is so hard (because I'm skipping some puzzles)
4. Stop playing the game for four years
6. Buy The Witness sometime in those four years
7. Play The Witness only recently because I saw Faker stream it online
8. Realize that through The Witness, I like well designed puzzle/logic games and I'm mesmerized by Jonathan Blow (designer and developer for Braid and The Witness)
9. Return to Braid after hitting a plateau in The Witness and delete the Steam save
10. Solve all worlds and beat the game
11. And then mind blown (to avoid spoilers)

If you are frustrated with the puzzles, quit the game. Maybe you're not in the right mindset for this game. I certainly wasn't when I stopped playing four years ago. This time around, I was in the mood after discovering that the designer for The Witness was the creator of Braid. Of course this was the opposite way around, because most people are introduced to Braid first, realize Jonathan Blow is a genius, then buy The Witness afterwards. Instead, I knew he was a genius through The Witness, then remembered I never fully finished Braid. I would occasionally mutter to myself the game design was "so efficient" (in both games). What I really mean by that is that nothing is "just there." In The Witness, there is no environmental facet that can be misconstrued as part of the game mechanic. Likewise, there is nothing in Braid designed to throw you off or waste your time, aka red herring. There isn't a single action that felt like a waste of time. A lot of Jonathan Blow's design philosophy is on the internet and Wikipedia, but that part about red herrings is implicit in the gameplay alone.

This shouldn't need to be stated, but I'll say it anyway. If you don't like puzzle games, don't buy it. Or buy it and realize you're not in the right mindset to solve puzzles? Kind of annoying seeing thumbs down when the reviewer quit the game because it was hard, not because it was tedious (you don't even know).

I'm glad I didn't look up a guide to solve Braid four years ago. I only had to look up one puzzle for this recent playthrough. Instead, I got through it in a few sittings. Once again, I also regret looking up sneak peeks and other people's playthroughs in The Witness. Don't look up guides for Jonathan Blow's games. [b]TLDR[/b] Braid still provides some hours of fun and challenging - and occasionally frustrating - puzzles, although I feel that nowadays there are better offers within the genre. [18/20⭐, 10h🏅, 3/5💡]

[b]Context[/b] I’ve played Braid back when it came out, and to be honest, the game never really clicked with me back then. When revisiting it after all these years, and often seeing it lists of greatest games in the meantime, I was kind of hoping for a "how could I have been so blind" moment. But it never came. Not that I have anything bad to point out either. 

[b]Writing[/b] The player controls a character that is revisiting and reinterpreting his story with a "princess". The story didn’t really do anything for me. I’m all for obscure and ambiguous plots, but here the story felt so disconnected from the actual gameplay that it felt forced. (There are several theories online, none particularly convincing.) 

[b]Aesthetics[/b] The visuals and soundtrack are pleasing, but again nothing really memorable.

[b]Gameplay[/b] The main mechanic of the game is controlling how time flows, and is connected to the narrative. The puzzles are challenging enough, medium-hard, and each world introduces a different mechanic to time control that keeps the game fresh. But for some reason I didn’t feel the satisfaction I often feel in other games when finally solving a difficult puzzle. Probably because of some precision and timed puzzles, which are really not my cup of tea. You can die, but can rewind to any previous state, so no gameovers. The game auto-saves, but mid-level progress is not saved.

[b]Value[/b] It took me 10h to complete all achievements, which is not particularly long, but it included some additional playthroughs for the last achievement. You can revisit previous worlds and levels, and there are multiple progress slots. There is an alternative ending depending on finding secrets. There is a speedrun achievement which is not trivial, and, of course, may require additional playthroughs. Other than that, achievements are related to completing the levels. Replay value for the story and revisiting the same puzzles.

PS: I absolutely hate speedrun achievements in puzzle platform games, if that's really what the developers are expecting players to master, I'm really not the target audience. In retrospective, this might have affected my review.

At first glance Braid looks like a typical Mario platformer where we jump on the incoming enemies. In fact, the main protagonist, Tim, is searching for a princess (captured by a monster). Now, all this looks pretty familiar up until the point you die for the first time. The screen is suddenly frozen and you realise that with a press of a button you can reverse time. So, Tim cannot actually die and reversing time allows us to make a better jump or simply make a different decision.

Time manipulation affects some of the things around us in a different way. It is possible that the reversal speed for some is not identical than it is for others. So, this ability is not only for making sure we cannot fail the game but in later stages it will be a must in order for us to make progress. And this is another characteristic of Braid: it can be pretty challenging, time manipulation or not.

All this is accompanied by some excellent music and a graphic design that looks as if the game had been painted. Between stages texts allow us to understand more of the story (along with Tim's feelings and emotions). Progress is also presented in an interesting way: later stages can already be entered. The emphasis is on finding pieces of a jigsaw puzzle that we eventually need to complete. We go back and forth and by adding another piece to make the puzzle more complete a new area becomes accessible.

This an exceptionally great game which is not only for fans of the genre but for those who like challenging gameplay.
Has great visuals, features well-designed and enjoyable puzzles, and explores interesting themes through its gameplay and story.

While Braid is certainly ambitious and an overall net positive to gaming as a whole, I cannot recommend this title.

Maybe the most transformative game I've played. Braid introduced me to video games that can be so deeply affecting, not just from the story, but from the mechanics themselves. Braid is what brought me into video games as a lover of deep, compelling storytelling.

[i]Braid[/i] is a puzzle-platformer. The first smash hit of indie darling developer Jonathan Blow, this puzzler holds up well over a decade since its release thanks to its groundbreaking time manipulation mechanic. With a unique feel and a truly deep series of puzzles and secrets tied to time, this classic deserves a play. The high difficulty curve for learning the basics of time travel may put off some players, but those with a bit of tenacity will be met with a rewarding experience.

This game stars Tim, a besuited man who wakes up in an unreal world. Tasked with locating a missing princess, Tim must venture through multiple worlds of levels filled with traps and enemies. The catch? Tim can reverse time. Using this single power and a basic jump, scale through nearly fifty puzzle-filled areas chock full of collectibles and secrets. With each world introducing a new mechanic that makes puzzles ever the more complicated, how far can you last in this mind-bending adventure?

[i]Braid[/i]'s time manipulation mechanics are truly a unique spectacle to behold while playing. Even after hours, the unfamiliarity of balancing the rewind function with resuming at the right time to not die immediately again is still present. While some fun, reality-bending effects like [i]Portal[/i]'s portals become second nature to the player rather quickly (as there is a certain level of familiarity with other videogame warping mechanics), this game's oddity remains a testament to how ahead of the curve it was and still is.

Be forewarned: this is a mature puzzle game that does not guide the player by the hand. The basic gameplay design is a deceptively simple one, as most levels can just be walked through from start to finish with little obstruction. The real challenge comes in the form of optional puzzle pieces, of which there are twelve in each world. These pieces require stretching the logic of reversed time to its limits, as well as the various special gimmicks introduced in each world. Offering compounding degrees of complexity, what can be a very short game for the most genius/uninterested players will likely span quite a few hours.

[i]Braid's[/i] story boasts surprising depth tied to the game's infamous deep secrets. Most of the game's lore is delivered via storybooks at the beginning of each world, in short and subtle passages. But the game's true narrative only comes from the most dedicated of searching, the most intense applications of time-reversing powers - it is so beyond the pale for the scope of this videogame that, truly, most players would be better off seeking instruction online. But just as the optional puzzles require greater focus than average, the deepest secrets here will be sure to please those with an insatiable desire to undertake extreme investigative work in pursuit of the truth.

For its age and potentially short length, [i]Braid[/i] may be asking for a lot at full price. But during a sale this is an easy buy for those seeking a puzzle challenge, or a unique time-bending gameplay conceit. Jon Blow's magnum opus remains quite impressive long after its release, and there is little reason to believe it will change anytime soon.  [i]Braid[/i] gets an A.

I first learned of Braid from the “Mario is too Mainstream” sketch by Dorkly.  It didn’t color my opinion because I unsubbed from Dorkly years ago when they started pushing “Kevin the Assistant,” but when I read some of the flowery language used in the lore dumps, I was worried that maybe they had a point when they made Braid out to be pretentious Mario.  However, Dorkly was too busy projecting their own smugness onto the game and equating inspiration with copying to stick any real jabs to Braid.

That isn’t to say Braid isn’t a little smug.  The writing is self-indulgent, the twist is telegraphed so early that it doesn’t come as much of a shock, as the possibility had been planted in my head from the start.  As subversive as it once was, it feels its age, considering what it’s deconstructing (Super Mario Bros.) and how it characterizes its protagonist (romantic, melancholic, probably alcoholic).  It’s not unintelligent, it has something important to say, it’s just little on the nose and navel-gazy, outdone in narratology by countless successors in the indie scene it helped shape.

The presentation is generally good.  The painterly graphics are nice and colorful, but occasionally get a bit cluttered with some of the puzzle layouts.  The music is peaceful and unobtrusive, while the sound effects are… odd.  The not-Goombas sound like ordinary guys and jumping on enemies sounds like an elastic band, but what really got me were the turtle-bunnies’ annoying stock cat noises, and the “strum” death sound effect makes me think of the Taco Bell “bong” for some reason.  I think it’s the rewind reverb.

Ultimately, it’s the puzzles that really make the game worthwhile.  The platforming is a bit underwhelming, and the game doesn’t make the most out of all of its mechanics, but the rewind ability and the other effects surrounding it are really fun to play with, and the puzzles are rewarding to figure out.  The last level, though it didn’t shock me from a narrative standpoint, also played fantastically.

The rougher elements might make you want to wait for a sale, or maybe consider checking out the anniversary edition; I don’t know how improved it is.  Considering how it's aged, I can't say Braid is a masterpiece, but I'd say it's still worth playing after almost two decades.

Then you drop it on a cloud to slow it so the cannon fires a second cloud. Then you drop it under another gate to slow it down, then under a pipe with a not-Piranha Plant so you can go through without being bitten, then on two cannons so they fire slower, then under a ladder so you can climb it before it falls all the way down, but it's all so in-your-face and isolated from the rest of the levels it doesn't feel satisfying or rewarding to do so. There is one clever puzzle in World 6 that requires the ring to fall down at the same time as a key so you have time to run and grab it before it falls off, but that's about the only one. World 4, arguably the hardest world (screw that last key level), has the most "puzzly" mechanic in the entire game, and the only one that actually gets explored a fair amount (probably because it imposes such a massive limitation on what you can do with gameplay and level design, forcing actual puzzles to be designed around it).
    [*]Adding [i]once again[/i] to that, you'd imagine that a puzzle game would evolve its mechanics so that the endgame is a culmination of everything you've learned thus far. This game doesn't do that. Mechanics are like Donkey Kong Country level gimmicks in that they get dropped almost as soon as they are introduced. This is fine in traditional platformers, but in a puzzle game it just leads to an empty feeling, like neither you nor the game ever grow.
    [*]The music is okay, or at least I assume it is, because the game really doesn't want you listening to it, as every time you make use of the time mechanics (which is all the time) the music also gets warped.
    [*]The Mario elements in this game (not-Goombas, not-Yoshis, not-Piranha Plants, flags at the end of certain levels, "the Princess is in another castle"...) feel extremely random, like the developer chose them just to bring some sense of familiarity/nostalgia to boost sales while doing absolutely nothing meaningful with them within the game itself. It's all meaningless. The feeling I got was that it was done just for the sake of being "subversive", which I guess did work in this game's favor as it probably wouldn't have been so popular with the gaming journalists as a "masterpiece" had those elements been replaced with something original that actually suited this game's tone.
[/list]
All in all, while I appreciate this game's impact on the indie scene and how it served as an inspiration for so many developers, this is not a fun game. It reeks of pretentiousness. No wonder it took me five years to 100% it; it wasn't just because I assumed the speedrun would be far too time-consuming (no pun intended), it was also because I just did not want to play this again [i]period[/i].

But that pain is worth the payoff of finally being able to figure out a puzzle after spending an hour steaming at the ears. You feel like a God, until you reach the next puzzle. 

But the best payoff of all is the twist at the end of the story. The story is primarily told through books read at the beginning of each world. The writing in this game is extremely contemplative and existential, dealing with topics like memories, identity, and the nature of relationships. The writing beautifully weaves into the timetravel mechanics for each world. The design of the mechanics, their ability to be relevant to the story, and their ability to make the game's puzzles more complex at the same time, is the product of genius. The story, like a poem, doesn't explain itself. It leaves itself open to interpretation. The replayability of this game is in the different meanings that can be thought of upon further playthroughs of the game.

The music of the game fits the aestitic of the art style and reflects the mood of the story very well. The gravity of the twist near the end of the story is helped by the music. The music plays a role in telling the game's story.

In conclusion, this game is the greatest puzzle platformer because it ties the story, gameplay mechanics, and music together SO WELL that I would go back in time to experience the game all over again for the first time (small Braid joke). If you like puzzle platformers and you don't buy this game, WHAT ARE YOU EVEN DOING?

Definitely one of the best games out there period. Always loved puzzle games, always loved platformers, so obviously this game is perfect for me. I really think this game is a great entry-way for anyone who is interested in either of those two genres however, or would simply like to try one. This game really teaches you how to think outside the box, and just when you think you've gotten a new mechanic understood properly, it throws a new one at you to continue to keep you on your toes. It has a very fair curve and never gets too mechanically difficult, all of its puzzles are solved through the mind and because of this it is one of the most fair platformers I have ever played. 

The rewind mechanic is absolutely wonderful to use, mistakes simply get reversed in a few seconds, and you can keep playing like nothing happened. Accidentally missed a jump? Rewind back to try again until you make it. Died to a goomba? Rewind and kill that sucker. Not only does it take away the punishing aspect that most platformers have, but it allows the game to implement so many wonderful concepts and mechanics that push the limits of what you're capable of using this rewind feature. I don't want to spoil what any of the puzzles or mechanics are, but this game really goes above and beyond with providing fascinating lateral puzzles for you to work your brain around, and when you eventually finish this game, you'll feel like a champion. My only criticism for the game would have to be that some concepts aren’t used enough, where there’s so much more room for unique puzzles but it doesn’t really do too much with it. Thankfully there’s always mods or custom levels that can solve this issue!

While this game isn't too dense in gameplay, it is extremely dense in potential. Once you grasp all of the simple mechanics, you could easily beat the game in less than an hour (in fact, one of the achievements is to do it in 45 minutes). However, there are so many potential ways of optimization that you'll find yourself accidentally speedrunning the game just by finding new methods to beating older levels. Even after you've fully understood everything there is to know regarding the game and its puzzles/mechanics, you'll still keep coming back just to master them even more, or to try to beat the game faster than you have before. This game never gets old to me, and everyone I have shown this game to feels the same way.

Of course, a necessary component for a good game is also its story and soundtrack, and don’t worry, for they’re both excellent in this game. Before you start each “world”, you are placed in a room that contains many books for you to read if you care about the story and meaning behind the game, and the writing is absolutely brilliant. I won’t spoil any of the story, but it has a brilliant meaning behind it all, and you’ll be engrossed in the words after you beat the game. As for the soundtrack, it is extremely pleasant to listen to. It is a peacefully orchestrated soundtrack that adds a really nice background to each level. While the game isn’t built to be frustrating, it can always be tough figuring out a puzzle, and instead of flashing intense music at your face to lower your focus levels, you get to hear majestic piano or violin to help you focus. 

Trust me, this is more than worth your money.

I wanted to like Braid. It's a game that begs to be liked: beautiful, painting-like art, soothing soundtrack, and ingeniously crafted puzzles. It has a complex, well-written storyline that requires a series of intelligent inferences to follow, as well as a whole horde of subtext and interpretation articles written by people far more intelligent than me. It's an intimidating game, too: a game that birthed an entire genre and has become a sort of initiation into indie gaming for many players out there. It's one of those games that, when you're having a conversation about small developer teams and the rise in indie gaming, you just can't ignore.

A lot of people make the mistake of equating an industry changing game with a good game, and while Braid is, in truth, a work of art, I struggle to qualify it at as a truly enjoyable experience as a game. The mechanics of Braid revolve around the idea of time-manipulation as a core gameplay element. When your character moves forward, time moves forward. If your character moves backwards, time moves backward. But what starts as a relatively simple and unique method of creative puzzle solving turns into something grotesquely twisted and almost indecipherably complicated. Hard puzzles in a game should never be a bad thing, but puzzles that are so far out of the realm of my thinking that they become nigh unsolvable aren't fun, they're incredibly off-putting.

On top of the intensely challenging puzzle-solving aspect of Braid, the game also identifies as a platformer that often tests the reflexes and timing of the player holding the controller. As the game progresses the player must become more and more precise with their control of the main character. Unfortunately, this, in combination with the difficult puzzles, made for a game that I could only play half of—any of the puzzles that weren't too farfetched for me to understand were instead doubly frustrating because they required a precision and sense of timing that my fumbling hands just couldn't seem to fathom.

Altogether, Braid's the kind of game whose phenomenal story is somewhat ruined by its gameplay for me. It's the sort of game that I would rather watch someone play through on YouTube and then read about it on the wiki afterwards than sit down with the controller myself. It's a summary game—the kind of thing that when you step back and look at it as a whole, it's a wonderfully enlightening experience, but that experience is drowned out by an incredibly steep learning curve and absurdly convoluted puzzle solutions. Playing Braid is an uphill climb and while the view at the top of that mountain is pretty great, it's not quite worth the struggle to get to it in the first place.

Braid is a classic indie darling, a puzzle platformer that inspired hundreds to make their own sidescrolling adventures. Before anything else, Braid's presentation is a painterly aesthetic mixed with a semi-philosophical backdrop, on par for the developer's work. My main issue with the game is that the game never truly gates progress until the very end. Braid allows you to damn near walk to the exit in many of the levels, permitting you to skip most of the actual challenge of the game, which is solving the puzzle pieces. Unfortunately, the process itself is not fun. Many of the mechanics are too complicated for their own good, and some moments felt more like I needed to stand in a very specific place or platform well enough to complete a puzzle rather than actually work a solution. The story is quite good, but even as short as the game is, I wanted it to be over more times than not. That said, I don't think it's a bad game at all, and just take it at your own pace.
